title: Pitfalls in Neuroimaging of Headache: A Case Report and Review of the Literature
case_prompt: A 74-year-old man presented with a one-year history of persistent right-sided headache affecting the frontotemporooccipital region. The headache was daily, with an intensity of 4/10, described as a dull ache with occasional brief shooting retroorbital pain once or twice a week and occasional photophobia. There was no nausea, visual dysfunction, or exacerbation by postural changes or Valsalva maneuvers. The headache failed to settle with analgesics. He had a history of migraine in his teens with the last episode 10 years ago and a family history of migraine. His medical history included ischemic heart disease, diabetes mellitus, and COPD. Physical and neurological examinations were normal. The differential diagnosis included hemicrania continua and chronic migraine, and a trial of indomethacin was initiated. A non-contrast CT scan of the brain showed age-related cerebral atrophy with no intracranial abnormality. The patient was treated for migraine, but “The response to the standard prophylactic and therapeutic treatment for migraine was suboptimal and variable.”
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Hemicrania continua was considered but an indomethacin trial did not confirm the diagnosis — “A trial of indomethacin with a starting dose of 25 mg was given and the dose was titrated slowly upward weekly depending on his tolerability and his INR.”  
2. Chronic migraine was considered given his past history and family history, but it was questioned after prophylactic treatment yielded only a “suboptimal and variable” response.  
3. An intracranial structural lesion was considered and initial non-contrast CT scanning was performed but “showed age related cerebral atrophy with no intracranial abnormality.”  
4. When oropharyngeal carcinoma was later diagnosed, brain metastasis was considered, yet multidisciplinary review concluded “that brain metastasis from the oropharyngeal cancer was unlikely.”  
5. Meningioma emerged as the cause when contrast-enhanced CT “identified a 4 cm enhancing mass in the right middle cranial fossa in keeping with a sphenoidal ridge meningioma,” and ultimately “The headache is thought to be secondary to meningioma.”
